prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength allow frequency to be measured at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B041 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, my case rests on three points an experimentalist can check. First, Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a specific invention that removes the lattice light shift on the clock transition, so that thousands of neutral atoms are probed at once with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. That is what moved optical clocks from one-ion statistics to ensemble statistics. Second, Ye's group realised the concept at the 10^-18 level in systematic uncertainty and stability, and used it to resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre scales and to explore many-body effects in the clock. Third, the result has been reproduced and intercompared in independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), which is the test I trust most. The chair's question about a citation is answerable: it should name the lattice at the magic wavelength as the invention and the 10^-18 realisation as the demonstrated outcome, and it should not mention clocks or frequency combs in general. That separates it from 2005 (the comb as a counter of optical cycles) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems, ions and photons). Support from five members of different specialties, and no one arguing that the maturity or the two-name credit fails, does not decide the matter for me, but it does mean the scientific objections have been tested.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is the one Danielsson and Eriksson press, that this is a better measurement rather than a new phenomenon, and that the fundamental-physics payoff is so far null results on constants and dark matter. I do not think that disqualifies it, but I accept it is a judgment about what the prize rewards and not a fact I can prove. A second weakness is credit: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the shift theory, early demonstrations and accuracy evaluation, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. The citation should therefore claim only the concept and the record-level realisation. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened and the best uncertainty figures keep improving, so some of the practical payoff is still ahead.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the lattice clock's discovery content lies in instrumentation and that the fundamental-physics payoff is mostly promised, while his own first choice is B004 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: I think the dividing line between instrument and discovery is less sharp than your argument needs. The magic-wavelength condition is a physical insight about differential light shifts, not a engineering refinement, and what followed (millimetre-scale redshift resolved in a lattice, collisional and many-body shifts studied in a controlled spin system) is observed physics. I agree that the constants and dark-matter results are null so far, so I would not put them in the citation. On B004, your own concession carries weight for me. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation behind Molenkamp's experiment and Hasan is tied to the 3D case, and with a three-name limit there is no set that avoids leaving out a principal. I cannot judge the Z2 invariant as well as you can, but a prize whose credit you yourself describe as imperfect is harder to defend than one with two uncontested names. I would ask you whether the clean-before-and-after argument you make for B004 is not equally met by a clock that changed what can be measured.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, argues that the existence of correlated phases and not their origin is the discovery, and concedes that optical lattice clocks are unquestionably mature.
responses.response: I appreciate that you separate the existence of the phases from their mechanism, and the comparison with high-Tc superconductors is fair in structure. Where I disagree is on timing and on what is stable. Eight years after the 2018 experiments the phase diagram is still moving, sample-to-sample variation is large, and the superconducting state is not understood, which is the opposite of the situation for the clock, where the key quantities (shifts, uncertainty budgets) are measured and reproduced between laboratories. A citation restricted to flat bands and correlated insulators with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero would be better than one including the superconductivity, but it would still rest on follow-up work by Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others whose claims it leaves out. I take your point that your own field's weighting may be generous, and I would add that mine is too, which is why I check the lattice clock against what Pearce, a non-AMO member, and Danielsson and you question, not only against what atomic physicists find natural.

responses.point: Johansson wants the B041 citation to lead with the clocks and the concept and to avoid a priority argument, treats the fundamental-physics payoff as prospective, and has disclosed proximity to the B028 community.
responses.response: I agree with the drafting principle and have moved my citation to follow it: it names the invention (the lattice at a magic wavelength) and the demonstrated result (10^-18), and says nothing about tests of fundamental physics or the redefinition of the second, since those are not yet delivered. I would not mention Lemonde, Takamoto or the institutes in the text, but the committee's public explanation of the prize can acknowledge them. On B028, I still think circuit QED is foundational, and I would not call the 2025 prize a bar because the subject differs, coupling to photons against macroscopic tunnelling. My difficulty is the four-name credit. Excluding Blais, who led the 2004 proposal, is hard to defend, and excluding Girvin or Schoelkopf is no easier. Combined with your own disclosure, that is why B028 stays an alternative and not my lead.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B041 with a citation naming the 10^-18 level, calls B034 credit messy, and prefers that the lattice concept be explicit in the wording.
responses.response: I agree with your concern about credit in B034 and it is why I would not use it as a second part: Chu is absent from the supplied names, and Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich overlap in a way that a three-name list cannot fix. It remains my first alternative only because the measurement content is strong. On the citation, I would keep the lattice and the magic wavelength explicit, because a wording based only on the accuracy level would invite a priority argument with the ion-clock groups and with NIST and PTB. I do not share your hesitation over whether a metrology prize is acceptable this year: the 2012 ion-clock prize recognised the control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is about a different regime of many atoms in a lattice, and I would say so in the explanation.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B027 (Young, Halperin, Nelson), calls it mature with clean authorship, concedes the 2016 overlap and first-order melting in some real systems, and lists B041 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the authorship of B027 is unusually clean and that the theory is mature, and I am glad B041 is your first alternative. My difficulty is the one you flag yourself: the 2016 prize for topological defects and defect-driven transitions makes it likely that the decisive insight will be judged covered, and the experimental picture in real systems is mixed, with first-order melting for hard disks. As an experimentalist I would also want an experimental confirmation that is as decisive as the clock comparisons, and the colloidal and simulation work does not yet play that role for all systems. If the committee decides on a theory prize this year, B027 would be a coherent choice, but I do not see the evidence of overlap-free novelty that would put it above B041.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement prize as discovery-grade, given the reservation about instrument versus new phenomenon that Danielsson and Eriksson hold. This is a question about the prize's criteria, not an unknown fact.

Whether the exact wording of the citation, especially the phrase on the lattice at a magic wavelength, is enough to prevent a priority dispute with Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups. I have not independently verified the chronology of the first demonstrations.
The latest uncertainty figures at the 10^-18 level and the status of the redefinition of the second were not checked against sources, and may have moved.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B041 or its credited names. As disclosed in round 1, during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, within the JILA environment where Ye works. That was a visit, not a collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I still do not consider it grounds for recusal. My WACQT role touches the Chalmers community relevant to B028, which I do not prefer; I keep B028 only as an alternative and would count Johansson's B028 support accordingly. I have no ties to any other shortlisted candidate.
